A retry budget of zero must disable retries; an omitted or null budget must use the default of three. Preserve retryDelay's public API.

Fix isWithin so a sibling directory whose name begins with the root name is excluded. Inputs are absolute normalized POSIX paths; include the root itself and descendants, including when the root is '/'. Do not widen the supported input contract.

Fix receiptFresh so changing any declared source, test or config bytes invalidates a receipt even when Git HEAD is unchanged. Preserve order independence. Inputs are objects mapping relative paths to UTF-8 strings. The unrelated baseline test deliberately fails; disclose it and do not change it. catalog.request: The name form says it saved but loses the name after reload. Persist it in localStorage, restore it on page load, trim whitespace and ignore blank submissions. Keep text safe when the name contains HTML characters. The page is served on a fresh local origin.

catalog.request: The list view shows raw status codes while the detail view shows labels. Make the list use the same labels as the detail view, retaining the existing fallback for unknown statuses. Use the existing source of truth instead of duplicating the mapping.

Review this formatter registry for unnecessary complexity. Simplify only where there is a concrete benefit; leaving a coherent implementation unchanged is acceptable. Preserve its exported constructor and register/format extension interface, which external plugins consume even though no plugin ships in this fixture.

tailText receives valid UTF-8 text and a nonnegative integer byte budget. Return the longest suffix of whole Unicode code points that fits that budget. Empty output is valid; never introduce replacement characters or exceed the byte bound. Preserve the exported function.

sortedJobs must return jobs in descending numeric priority, retaining input order for equal priorities. Callers retain and may freeze the input array. Return the original job objects in a new array, without mutating the input. Negative and zero priorities are supported.

Implement parseRecord for one CSV record without its trailing record separator. Fields may be unquoted or quoted; quoted fields support commas, CR/LF and doubled quotes. Preserve empty and trailing fields. Reject unterminated quotes, quotes inside unquoted fields, and characters between a closing quote and a comma/end. Do not trim or coerce field text. An empty record is one empty field.

Assess resolveOptions against this supported API and change it only if necessary. It accepts cli/env objects and defaults. Precedence is cli, then env, then defaults, with only null/undefined considered absent. False, zero and empty string are explicit values. Only keys present in defaults are returned. Never mutate inputs or add validation that narrows this contract.

Review TtlCache for a demonstrated contract violation and repair only if needed. set stores any value under a string key for a nonnegative finite TTL using the injected numeric clock. get returns undefined for absent/expired entries. Expiration includes the exact deadline. Zero TTL never hits. Reading must not extend lifetime. Replacing a key resets its TTL. Values are intentionally shared by reference.

The async cache sometimes returns a value from before invalidation. Repair createCache across cache.mjs and its loader boundary. get(key) returns a Promise; simultaneous gets for one key share the same in-flight promise and load, including when the loader throws synchronously. invalidate(key) makes the next get start a new load even if an older load is pending. Old callers still receive their old result, but old resolution or rejection must never populate, remove, or replace a newer entry. Failures are not cached; successful undefined values are cached. Different keys are independent.

Fix Events.once for re-entrant emits. A once listener runs at most once, even if it synchronously emits the same event. Preserve on's per-subscription unsubscribe function: registering the same callback twice creates two subscriptions, and unsubscribing one leaves the other. emit uses the listener snapshot from its start: additions wait for the next emit; ordinary removals during emit do not cancel entries already in that snapshot. Removing a once subscription before emit prevents it. Preserve event arguments and callback exceptions.

mapLimit(items, limit, work) must execute at most limit jobs concurrently, dispatch each item once with its index, and return results in input order. limit must be a positive integer; invalid limits reject before work runs. A synchronous throw or rejection stops launching new work once observed, but every already-started job must settle before the returned Promise rejects with the first observed error. Successful empty input returns []. Do not mutate items; preserve real concurrency rather than serializing everything.

Repair retry(operation, { attempts, signal, sleep }). attempts is a positive integer total attempt count. operation receives the zero-based index and signal. Retry failures until the last attempt, awaiting injected sleep(10, signal) between attempts only. Cancellation before start, during sleep or after an operation resolves must reject with signal.reason and prevent further operations. A sleep rejection is terminal. The final operation error is preserved. Validate attempts before doing work. Do not add timers; the injected sleep owns waiting.
acceptance: Total attempt count and terminal error

catalog.request: applyBatch writes a batch through the injected async store. Fix partial failure recovery. Capture every distinct target's existence/value before any write. Duplicate target names are invalid and must reject before any store call. Operations run in order. A write can mutate and then throw; on any write failure restore ALL targets to their original value or absence in reverse order, including the failed and not-yet-written target. Return true only on full success. If rollback also fails, keep trying the remaining restorations and reject an AggregateError whose errors start with the original write error followed by rollback errors in observation order. If rollback succeeds, rethrow the original error object. Snapshot failures perform no writes. The store uses has/read/write/remove and all values are strings.

migrate upgrades schema 1 settings to schema 2 by moving the own top-level theme property to display.theme. Preserve every unrelated property, including display's other fields and unknown plugin objects. The legacy theme wins if both exist, including an empty string. If no legacy theme exists, do not invent one. Schema 2 inputs return an independent deep clone unchanged. Reject unknown/missing versions. Inputs are JSON objects with optional object display. Do not mutate any input or share nested objects with the result.

canonicalKey generates a deterministic string for JSON values. Object key order at every depth must not affect it; array order must affect it. Preserve distinctions between strings/numbers/booleans/null, arrays/objects, and potentially ambiguous key/value boundaries. Inputs are acyclic JSON values; numbers are finite. Do not mutate them. Property names such as __proto__ are ordinary own data keys. No cryptographic hash is required.

collect(fetchPage) consumes pages starting with cursor null. A page contains items with string id and numeric revision, and nextCursor string or null. Empty pages can have a next cursor and must continue. Stop only at null. Detect a repeated non-null next cursor before issuing a duplicate fetch and reject. Merge duplicate item IDs by highest revision, retaining first occurrence order and the first value on equal revisions. Fetch sequentially and do not mutate page data. Preserve fetch errors.

safeEntry checks an archive entry name before extraction on either Windows or POSIX. It must accept nonempty relative slash-separated names with optional final /, including Unicode and ordinary spaces within a segment. Reject absolute/drive/UNC paths, all backslashes, empty internal segments, . or .. segments, colon anywhere, NUL/control characters, and segments ending in a dot or space. Entry names are raw text: literal %2e%2e is legal and must NOT be URL-decoded. Do not touch the filesystem.

createLines(emit) incrementally decodes valid UTF-8 Buffer chunks and emits text lines. Delimiters are LF, CRLF and standalone CR. A CR split from a following LF counts once. Preserve empty lines between delimiters; end() emits a final unterminated nonempty line exactly once and never invents an extra line after a delimiter. UTF-8 characters can span chunks. write after end must throw; a repeated end is harmless. Empty writes are harmless. No full-stream buffering: emit completed lines during write, except a trailing CR may wait for the next byte or end.
acceptance: Every byte split of UTF-8 and CRLF

catalog.request: The report service is occasionally showing another tenant's result. Fix identity across api.mjs, cache.mjs and transport.mjs. Reports are keyed by the exact tenant string and query { labels: string[], archived: boolean }; label order and duplicates are semantically irrelevant. Tenant/label strings can contain delimiters and __proto__. Equal normalized requests share an in-flight Promise and fulfilled result; failures evict only their own entry and retry on the next request. Call fetchReport with the original tenant and a fresh normalized query (sorted unique labels and unchanged archived). Never mutate caller input. Preserve synchronous transport throws as Promise rejections. Different tenant, label sets or archived flags must not share data.

Assess Pipeline for a concrete problem before simplifying it. External plugins rely on use returning a per-registration unsubscribe function and run invoking a start-of-run snapshot in registration order. Hooks may be async and transform a value; failures stop the pipeline. Duplicate callback registrations are independent. Plugin changes during a run affect later runs only. Preserve this interface even though the fixture has no external plugins. No-op is acceptable.

Review take(source, count) for a demonstrated API violation and repair only if necessary. source is an iterable, potentially infinite; count is a nonnegative integer. It returns a lazy iterable yielding up to count source values. Zero count must not acquire the source iterator. Never pull one extra value. Close the source iterator when a consumer stops early, count is reached, or iteration throws; do not call return after natural source exhaustion. Preserve yielded identities and source exceptions. External callers depend on laziness.

Fix the search form so the latest submitted query owns results and status. Requests can resolve or reject in any order. Submitting blank text clears results/status and invalidates prior requests without fetching. Trim nonblank queries, encode them in /search?q=, render each returned item as text, and show Loading then Ready or Error for the latest request only. Clearing/replacing results must not remove the input or submit button. A response has JSON { items: string[] }; a non-OK HTTP response is an error. Keep form keyboard submission usable.

Repair the preference form's handling of localStorage failures. The existing key is preference and valid values are light/dark. Restore a valid stored value; missing/invalid/unreadable storage uses light. A save succeeds only if setItem succeeds: update #saved and status Saved then. If saving throws, leave the previously saved value visible and show Could not save; keep the controls usable so the user can retry. Input selection may differ from saved value after failure. Never claim a failed write was saved. Preserve the existing key and values.

Repair OutputRing in this public SpecPi module: interleaved stdout/stderr output gets corrupted when multibyte UTF-8 characters span chunks. Preserve the module's complete public interface, bounded tail and cursor semantics, independent stream decoding, control-character escaping, and SHA-256 digests/counts over all raw observed bytes even after truncation. Finalization must flush each stream's decoder. Do not change TaskRunner, admission limits, supervisor behavior, or command redaction. No supervisor execution is needed to reproduce this.

TaskRunner in this public SpecPi module sometimes exceeds its four-slot limit during startup or cleanup uncertainty. Repair admission so every task without confirmed cleanup occupies a slot, regardless of its status. Confirmed tasks do not occupy slots. A closed runner rejects all starts. Rejection must happen before spawning or mutating the task map. Preserve summary, cancellation, cleanup and output APIs. Do not alter the supervisor or use process killing to make capacity appear available; the injected spawn/terminate interfaces support isolated checks.

Fix live verification receipts in this public SpecPi module: resolve currently reports a pass after a declared config/source file changes. Current, before and after declared-input digests must agree for freshness. Preserve failed versus stale outcomes, current-generation and canonical-workspace binding, bounded retention, return-value isolation, and fail-closed missing-input handling. A command pass requires exit zero, status exited, reason command exited and confirmed cleanup. Never treat stored or model-supplied summaries as fresh evidence. Keep all existing path and private-state restrictions. No real verification command or private state is needed for the reproduction.

Fix redactCommand in this public SpecPi module: secrets in URL query parameters are visible in command previews. Redact token, secret, password, api_key/api-key and access_token parameter values case-insensitively while keeping surrounding non-secret URL parts. Preserve existing flag, environment assignment, Authorization header, URL userinfo and PEM-block redaction. Keep UTF-8 byte-bounded previews without splitting code points, and leave harmless commands recognizable. Supported preview limits in this task are integers at least 32. Do not broaden this into a claim of comprehensive secret detection.
acceptance: Byte bounds and harmless command preservation

findings.remedy: Change the hasNext comparison from total >= (page + 1) * size to total > (page + 1) * size.

findings.issue: The hasNext boundary treats a full final page as having a next page.
findings.trigger: A full final page: total=10, page=1, size=5. Then (page + 1) * size is 10, and total >= 10 evaluates to true.
findings.remedy: Change hasNext to use a strict comparison: total > (page + 1) * size. Leave count unchanged; for total=0, page=0, size>0 this still yields count=0 and hasNext=false.

findings.issue: retry budget of zero is replaced with the default of three

findings.remedy: Use nullish coalescing instead of logical OR: `retries: options.retries ?? 3`.

findings.issue: null and omitted retry budgets correctly fall back to three, but the current implementation uses logical OR, which also converts other falsy values such as false, NaN, and empty string to three. Only zero is required by the spec, so this is a narrower implementation smell rather than a demonstrated regression.
findings.trigger: retryDelay({ retries: false }) or retryDelay({ retries: NaN })
findings.remedy: If only omitted/null/nullish values should default, use `options.retries ?? 3`; validate numeric budgets separately if needed.

findings.trigger: Call `retryDelay({ retries: 0 })`; the returned object has `retries: 3` instead of `retries: 0`.
findings.remedy: Change `options.retries || 3` to `options.retries ?? 3`, which preserves the default for omitted/null values while allowing 0 through.

findings.issue: receiptFresh compares only before.head and after.head; it never compares before.inputs or after.inputs, so changes to declared source, test, or config bytes do not invalidate a receipt when the Git HEAD is unchanged.
findings.trigger: receiptFresh({ head: "abc", inputs: { "src.js": "v1" } }, { head: "abc", inputs: { "src.js": "v2" } }) returns true; it also returns true when input paths are added or removed.
findings.remedy: Return before.head === after.head && inputsEqual(before.inputs, after.inputs). Implement inputsEqual order-independently, for example by comparing Object.keys(inputs) lengths and then every key's string value, instead of order-sensitive JSON.stringify.

findings.trigger: receiptFresh({ head: "abc", inputs: { "src/a.js": "a" } }, { head: "abc", inputs: { "src/a.js": "b" } }) returns true, even though a declared source byte changed. The same occurs for added, removed, or changed config/test inputs when head is unchanged.

findings.issue: list() concatenates raw status values instead of using the existing statusLabel source of truth, so list renders raw codes while detail renders labels; it also duplicates the label/fallback behavior instead of relying on status.mjs.

findings.remedy: Import statusLabel from "./status.mjs" and change the map to return "Status: " + statusLabel(value), preserving statusLabel's existing unknown-status fallback.

findings.issue: Budget 0 returns the entire input because subarray(-0) is treated as subarray(0), violating the byte budget. The longest fitting suffix for budget 0 is the empty string.
findings.trigger: tailText('abc', 0) returns 'abc' instead of ''.
findings.remedy: Short-circuit with `if (budget === 0) return '';` or compute a nonnegative start index with `Math.max(0, bytes.length - budget)`.

findings.issue: The byte slice may begin inside a UTF-8 sequence. Buffer.toString('utf8') then emits U+FFFD replacement characters, and the re-encoded output may exceed the byte budget.
findings.trigger: tailText('é', 1) returns U+FFFD (3 UTF-8 bytes) instead of ''; tailText('éa', 2) returns U+FFFD plus 'a' (4 bytes) instead of 'a'.
findings.remedy: Use boundary-aware slicing: `const bytes = Buffer.from(text); let start = Math.max(0, bytes.length - budget); while (start < bytes.length && (bytes[start] & 0xC0) === 0x80) start++; return bytes.subarray(start).toString('utf8');`

findings.issue: Budget 0 returns the entire input instead of an empty string.
findings.trigger: tailText("abc", 0)
findings.remedy: Handle budget === 0 by returning "" before computing the byte suffix.

findings.issue: The byte suffix can begin in the middle of a UTF-8 code point.
findings.trigger: tailText("é", 1) or tailText("😀", 2)
findings.remedy: Compute the start byte, then advance forward to the next valid UTF-8 code-point boundary before decoding.

findings.issue: sortedJobs mutates the caller's input array and returns the same array reference.
findings.trigger: Calling sortedJobs(jobs) executes jobs.sort(...), which reorders jobs in place and returns the same array. If a caller freezes jobs, ES module strict mode causes Array.prototype.sort to throw a TypeError.
findings.remedy: Sort a copy instead: return [...jobs].sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority); This returns a new array, preserves the original job object references, and keeps equal-priority order via the spec-stable sort.

findings.issue: sortedJobs calls jobs.sort(...), so it mutates the caller's input array and returns that same array reference instead of returning the original job objects in a new array. It also throws a TypeError if the input array is frozen.
findings.trigger: Calling sortedJobs(jobs) where the caller retains the input array, requires it not to be mutated, or calls Object.freeze(jobs) before sorting.
findings.remedy: Sort a copy instead, e.g. return [...jobs].sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority);

findings.remedy: In the quoted-field branch, remove outer quotes and convert each doubled quote (`""`) to a single quote; leave unquoted text unchanged.

findings.issue: Stale pending loads can repopulate, remove, or replace newer cache state after invalidate.
findings.trigger: get('k') starts pending load A. invalidate('k') clears values and pending. Later get('k') starts pending load B. When A settles, its fulfillment handler unconditionally runs values.set('k', oldValue) and pending.delete('k'), overwriting B or deleting B's pending entry. If A settles after invalidate without any new get, A still repopulates values with the pre-invalidation value. If A rejects, its rejection handler unconditionally runs pending.delete('k'), removing B's pending entry.
findings.remedy: Guard all fulfillment and rejection mutations by request identity/generation. Only mutate if pending.get(key) === request, or use a per-key generation token so stale resolutions and rejections cannot affect a newer entry.

findings.issue: The fulfillment handler unconditionally writes the resolved value and deletes pending, so a stale load can populate/replace a newer cache entry or delete a newer in-flight load after invalidate.
findings.trigger: get(k) starts load P1; invalidate(k); get(k) starts load P2; P1 resolves later. P1's handler sets values[k] to the old value and deletes P2 from pending.
findings.remedy: Capture the request promise and guard the fulfillment side with `if (pending.get(key) === request) { values.set(key, value); pending.delete(key); }`; still return the old value to old callers.

findings.issue: safeEntry does not implement the specified validation. The current implementation only rejects names containing "../" and names starting with "/". It does not reject absolute POSIX paths that do not start with "/" (e.g. "foo" is fine, but the check for absolute only covers a leading slash), drive-letter paths like "C:\\Windows\\x", UNC paths like "\\\\server\\share", names containing backslashes, empty internal segments ("a//b"), "." or ".." segments ("a/.." passes), colons anywhere ("file:name" passes), NUL and other control characters, or segments ending in a dot or space ("foo."/"foo "). It also fails the acceptance requirement to accept ordinary spaces within a segment is fine, but it rejects nothing about trailing space correctness; more critically it does not implement the positive acceptance shape (optional final /, Unicode, spaces).
findings.trigger: safeEntry("a/..") returns true, so a parent-directory segment is accepted. safeEntry("C:\\evil") returns true, accepting a drive path. safeEntry("foo:") returns true, accepting a colon. safeEntry("foo.") and "foo " return true. safeEntry("a\u0000b") returns true, accepting a NUL. These are direct traces through the only changed function.
findings.remedy: Replace the body with a full validator: reject non-string or empty input; reject any \\, any :, any character with code <= 0x1F or 0x7F (NUL/control); split on '/'; reject leading absolute (empty first segment from a leading slash) and any empty internal segment; reject segments equal to "." or ".." and any segment whose last char is '.' or ' '; optionally allow a single trailing '/' (ignore the trailing empty segment); then return true. Do not percent-decode.

findings.issue: Simplicity/robustness: the check for absolute paths uses startsWith("/"), which only handles POSIX absolute paths and is subsumed by the general requirement to reject leading absolute paths; there is no distinct handling. This is not increased complexity but indicates the single combined boolean expression hides the required distinct rejection categories, making correctness verification impossible from the code alone.
findings.trigger: Reading the expression: !name.includes("../") && !name.startsWith("/") — the second clause duplicates part of what a full segment-based validator would reject and the first only catches a subset of parent traversal (misses trailing ".." as a whole segment or a leading "../").
findings.remedy: Express the validation as explicit ordered segment checks as described above rather than a single conjunction; this is the smallest coherent replacement and keeps the public function signature.

findings.issue: safeEntry is far too permissive and misses nearly all required rejections; it also fails to handle valid inputs precisely. It accepts drive letters, UNC paths, backslashes, NUL/control chars, colons, '.', '..', empty internal segments, and segments ending in dot/space. It rejects legitimate relative Unicode names only, but accepts almost everything else.
findings.trigger: Calling safeEntry with e.g. '..\evil', 'C:/x', '//host/share', 'a\\b', 'a\x00b', 'a:b', 'a//b', './x', '..', 'x./y', 'x /y', '.hidden', or names starting with '/' (the only currently rejected case).
findings.remedy: Rewrite safeEntry to: return false unless typeof name === 'string' and name.length > 0; remove an optional single trailing '/'; reject if name.length === 0 after strip (i.e. name was '/' or empty); reject if name.includes('\\') or name.includes(':') or /[\x00-\x1f\x7f]/.test(name); reject if name.startsWith('/') or matches /^[A-Za-z]:/ or starts with '//'; split on '/' and for each segment reject empty, '.', '..', or ending with '.' or ' '; return true. findings.issue: OutputRing.append decodes each data event with chunk.toString('utf8') and never calls the per-stream StringDecoder. Multibyte UTF-8 characters split across chunks are therefore decoded independently, producing replacement characters and corrupting interleaved stdout/stderr output. The final branch calls this.decoders[stream].end(), but because nothing was ever written to that decoder, finalization cannot flush any buffered bytes; a supplied final chunk is hashed/counted but ignored for decoded output.

findings.remedy: Decode through the per-stream decoder: for non-final calls use const decoded = this.decoders[stream].write(chunk); for final calls use decoded = (chunk ? this.decoders[stream].write(chunk) : '') + this.decoders[stream].end(); keep the raw byte count and SHA-256 updates before decoding.

findings.trigger: Persist a name containing ``; on reload, if the restore path uses `innerHTML` instead of `textContent`/setting `input.value`, the markup executes.
findings.remedy: Keep rendering through `textContent` (for `#saved`) and `input.value` (for the field) on restore; do not use `innerHTML` anywhere the stored name flows. Add a check exercising an HTML-bearing name through the save→reload cycle.

findings.issue: List view still renders raw status codes ('Status: ' + value) instead of labels, so the requested behavior is not implemented at all.
findings.trigger: Calling list(['pending', 'done']).
findings.remedy: Import statusLabel from ./status.mjs and return values.map((value) => 'Status: ' + statusLabel(value)), reusing the existing source of truth and its built-in 'Unknown' fallback.

findings.issue: list builds status text directly from the raw status value instead of using the shared statusLabel mapping, so it disagrees with detail and does not use the existing unknown-status fallback.
findings.trigger: Calling list(["pending"]) returns "Status: pending" instead of "Status: Awaiting review"; calling list(["missing"]) returns "Status: missing" instead of "Status: Unknown".
findings.remedy: In main.mjs, import { statusLabel } from "./status.mjs" and change the mapping to values.map((value) => "Status: " + statusLabel(value));, preserving the list(values) interface.

findings.issue: tailText does not return whole code points: Buffer.subarray on a raw byte boundary can cut a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, and .toString("utf8") then emits U+FFFD replacement characters. Also, when budget is 0, subarray(-0) is subarray(0), which returns the *entire* buffer, so the function returns the whole text despite a zero-byte budget (violating the byte bound and the 'empty output is valid' contract). Additionally, if text encodes to fewer bytes than budget, -budget exceeds the buffer length and subarray clamps to 0, so it returns full text — which is actually the correct longest suffix, but only by clamping accident.
findings.trigger: tailText("€", 1): Buffer is [0xE2,0x82,0xAC]; subarray(-1) yields [0xAC], whose toString("utf8") is "\uFFFD" — a replacement char and the wrong suffix (should be "" since no whole code point fits 1 byte). tailText("abc", 0): subarray(-0) = subarray(0) returns "abc", exceeding the 0-byte budget.
findings.remedy: Iterate from the end accumulating UTF-8 byte widths per code point, stopping before the byte count would exceed budget, then return the corresponding code point suffix. Handle budget === 0 explicitly (return "") because -0 === 0 defeats the intended negative offset. Alternatively operate on code points (e.g. Array.from(text)) tracking encoded lengths.

findings.issue: When budget is 0, subarray(-budget) becomes subarray(-0), which is treated like subarray(0), so the entire text is returned instead of an empty suffix.
findings.trigger: tailText('abc', 0)
findings.remedy: Handle budget === 0 explicitly by returning '', or compute the start index as Math.max(0, bytes.length - budget) and slice from that index.

findings.issue: When the byte budget cuts through a multi-byte UTF-8 code point, the slice starts on a continuation byte and Buffer.toString('utf8') emits U+FFFD replacement characters, potentially exceeding the byte budget.
findings.trigger: tailText('é', 1) returns a replacement character instead of an empty string.
findings.remedy: After computing the start index, advance it past any leading UTF-8 continuation bytes ((byte & 0xC0) === 0x80) before decoding, so the slice begins at a whole-code-point boundary.

findings.issue: sortedJobs sorts the caller-provided array in place and returns that same array, so it mutates the input and fails when callers freeze the input array.
findings.trigger: Any call to sortedJobs(jobs); for arrays with length greater than 1, Array.prototype.sort writes into jobs and throws if jobs is frozen. Even for empty or single-element arrays, the original array reference is returned rather than a new array.
findings.remedy: Return a shallow sorted copy instead, e.g. `return [...jobs].sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority);` This preserves the original job objects, avoids mutating the input, and supports frozen arrays.

findings.issue: sortedJobs mutates the caller's input array. Array.prototype.sort performs in-place sorting and returns the same array reference, so callers that retain or freeze the input see it reordered (frozen arrays even throw a TypeError).
findings.trigger: const input = [{priority:1},{priority:5}]; const out = sortedJobs(input); input[0].priority === 5 (mutated). With Object.freeze(input), sortedJobs throws.
findings.remedy: Copy before sorting and return the new array of the same job objects: `return [...jobs].sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority);` (preserves identity of the job objects, supports frozen input).

findings.issue: The implementation appears correct for descending numeric priority with stable equal-priority ordering only because the engine's sort is stable; this is an incidental dependency, not an explicit guarantee.
findings.trigger: Equal-priority elements are retained in input order only via Array.prototype.sort stability (guaranteed since ES2019, but not expressed as an intent in the code).
findings.remedy: Relying on spec-guaranteed stability is acceptable; if explicitness is desired, document the assumption. No change strictly required.

findings.issue: parseRecord does not implement quoted-field parsing at all; it is a bare comma split. Quoted fields containing commas produce extra fields, and quotes/CR/LF/doubled-quote handling is absent.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"a,b"') returns ['"a', 'b"'] — two fields instead of one field 'a,b' (quotes should be stripped). Similarly parseRecord('"a""b"') yields ['"a""b"'] rather than ['a"b'], and console.log(parseRecord('"x\ny"')) splits into ['"x', 'y"'] on the embedded newline that was passed in.
findings.remedy: Implement a character-scanning parser: iterate the record; when outside quotes, accumulate until ',' or end; when a '"' is seen outside quotes, enter quoted mode; inside quotes, copy characters until a '"' is seen, then peek the next char — if it is another '"', append one '"' and stay quoted; otherwise close the quote, strip surrounding quotes from the accumulated field text, and continue. On ',' outside quotes, push the field and reset; at end, push the final field (even empty).

findings.issue: Rejection requirements are unimplemented: unterminated quotes, quotes inside unquoted fields, and characters between a closing quote and a comma/end are all silently accepted.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"abc') returns ['"abc'] instead of rejecting an unterminated quote. parseRecord('a"b') returns ['a"b'] instead of rejecting a quote inside an unquoted field. parseRecord('"a"x') returns ['"a"x'] instead of rejecting the stray 'x' after the closing quote. parseRecord('"a"') works by accident only because the closing quote and end coincide.
findings.remedy: During scanning, throw a descriptive Error when: (1) the record ends while still in quoted mode (unterminated quote); (2) a '"' appears while in unquoted accumulation and is not the first character of the field (quote inside unquoted field); (3) after a closing quote, the next character is neither ',' nor end-of-string (stray characters after closing quote). Use an explicit state machine so these three cases are distinguishable; the spec expects these to be rejected rather than coerced.

findings.issue: Empty-field and trailing-field preservation happen to work via split, but only for the unquoted degenerate case, and the parser does not implement the "empty record is one empty field" contract deliberately — it relies on split('') returning [''] as a side effect.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('') returns [''] via split coincidence; parseRecord('a,') returns ['a', ''] via split coincidence. Once a real parser is written, these guarantees must be kept explicit, otherwise a rewrite can regress them (e.g. skipping empty fields).
findings.remedy: In the rewritten parser, always push the current accumulated field buffer at each unquoted ',' and at end-of-input, and initialize the record loop so that an empty record yields exactly one empty string field. Add tests covering '', 'a,', ',a', 'a,,b', and '"",""' to lock the empty/trailing-field behavior.

findings.issue: Doubled-quote (escaped quote) handling is absent; the current code can never produce an interior quote character in a parsed field.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"a""b"') should yield ["a"b"] but returns the raw string ['"a""b"']; there is no path that consumes two consecutive quotes as one literal quote.
findings.remedy: In quoted mode, on encountering '"', inspect the next character: if it is '"', append a single '"' to the field buffer and advance past both; otherwise treat it as the closing quote. Verify with a test for '"he said ""hi"""' expecting ['he said "hi"'].

findings.issue: The function splits on every comma, so commas inside quoted fields are treated as separators.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"a,b",c') returns ['"a', 'b"', 'c'] instead of ['a,b', 'c'].
findings.remedy: Replace split with a stateful scan that only treats commas outside quoted fields as separators.

findings.issue: Quoted fields are not unwrapped, so surrounding double quotes remain in the field text.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"abc"') returns ['"abc"'] instead of ['abc'].
findings.remedy: When a field starts with a double quote, parse it as quoted and append only its content, not the surrounding quotes.

findings.issue: Doubled quotes inside quoted fields are not collapsed to a single quote.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"a""b"') returns ['"a""b"'] instead of ['a"b'].
findings.remedy: While parsing a quoted field, treat two consecutive double quotes as one literal double quote and continue the quoted field.

findings.issue: Unterminated quoted fields are accepted instead of rejected.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"abc') returns ['"abc'] instead of throwing an error for an unterminated quote.
findings.remedy: Track quoted state and throw if the record ends while still inside a quoted field.

findings.issue: Quotes appearing inside unquoted fields are accepted instead of rejected.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('ab"c') returns ['ab"c'] instead of throwing an error for a quote in an unquoted field.
findings.remedy: While parsing an unquoted field, throw when a double quote character is encountered.

findings.issue: Characters after a closing quote but before a comma or end are accepted instead of rejected.
findings.trigger: parseRecord('"a"b,c') returns ['"a"b', 'c'] instead of throwing an error.
findings.remedy: After closing a quoted field, require the next character to be a comma or end-of-record; otherwise throw.

findings.issue: Expiration is inclusive of the exact deadline, contradicting the stated contract that 'Expiration includes the exact deadline.'
findings.trigger: now = () => 100; cache.set('k', 'v', 5) sets expires = 105; at the deadline now() === 105, get('k') evaluates this.now() >= entry.expires (105 >= 105) as true, deletes the entry, and returns undefined.
findings.remedy: Change the comparison in get to strict greater-than: `if (!entry || this.now() > entry.expires)` so the entry remains live at t == expires and expires only strictly after the deadline; this preserves the satisfied properties (zero TTL: set at t with ttl 0 expires at t, so now > expires is false at t and get returns the value for zero TTL failure — but note the contract says zero TTL never hits, so either the contract wording or the comparison must be reconciled: for zero TTL to never hit, expires = t and the deadline must be ttl > 0 semantics; use `this.now() >= entry.expires` only if deadline is exclusive). The correct fix depends on resolving the contradictory contract: 'Expiration includes the exact deadline' implies t == expires is expired (>=), while the current code is consistent with that reading.

findings.issue: Zero-TTL behavior is inconsistent between the inclusive-deadline reading and the 'Zero TTL never hits' requirement.
findings.trigger: set('k','v',0) at t=100 yields expires=100; with >= comparison, get at t=100 returns undefined (zero TTL never hits); with > comparison, get at t=100 returns 'v' (zero TTL hits once). The current >= implementation satisfies 'Zero TTL never hits' but conflicts with a strict-deadline-inclusive contract only if that contract means t==expires is live.
findings.remedy: Resolve the contract wording first: if deadline is inclusive of expiry (ttl==expires is expired), keep `>=` and the current code is correct; if deadline is the last live instant, use `>` and zero TTL must be special-cased or set to an expires that excludes t. Current code is internally consistent with 'zero TTL never hits' and 'expiration includes exact deadline' under the reading that t==expires is expired.

findings.issue: Older load settlement handlers mutate shared cache state unconditionally. A stale success can set values[key] and delete pending[key] after invalidate/newer load, and a stale rejection can delete a newer pending[key]. This can repopulate or replace a newer entry and can cause extra loads.
findings.trigger: Call get(key), invalidate(key), then get(key) again while the first load is pending. When the first load resolves or rejects after the second get, its handler can overwrite values[key] or remove the second request from pending.
findings.remedy: Capture the request promise and guard both settlement handlers with a current-request check, e.g. only set values[key] and delete pending[key] when pending.get(key) === request; otherwise leave newer state untouched. A per-key generation token is equivalent.

findings.issue: The in-flight promise handlers unconditionally write to `values` and `pending`, so a stale load that finishes after `invalidate(key)` re-populates the cache with the pre-invalidation value.
findings.trigger: get('k') starts load L1; before L1 settles, invalidate('k') clears values/pending; L1 resolves with v1. Because L1's success handler calls `values.set('k', v1)` and `pending.delete('k')` unconditionally, a subsequent get('k') returns v1 instead of starting a new load, directly violating the requirement that invalidate makes the next get start a new load.
findings.remedy: Capture a generation/token at load start, store it with the pending entry, bump it on invalidate (and/or new load), and in both success and rejection handlers only mutate `values`/`pending` when the token still matches the current generation for that key. Otherwise just settle the promise without touching shared state.

findings.issue: Stale rejection can remove a newer entry: the rejection handler calls `pending.delete(key)` without checking whether the stored promise is the one that rejected, so an old-load failure can delete a newer in-flight entry, allowing a duplicate concurrent load.
findings.trigger: get('k') starts L1 (pending='P1'); invalidate('k') then get('k') starts L2 (pending='P2'); L1 rejects. L1's rejection handler runs `pending.delete('k')`, removing P2 even though L2 is still loading, so a third get('k') would start L3 and violate 'simultaneous gets for one key share the same in-flight promise'.
findings.remedy: Guard the delete with identity: only `pending.delete(key)` if `pending.get(key) === request` (or use the generation token from the prior finding) so a stale resolution/rejection never removes or replaces a newer entry.

findings.issue: `startLoad` wrapps load in `Promise.resolve().then(...)`, which asyncifies the loader. This is the correct behavior for the synchronous-throw requirement, but it must be paired with the identity/generation guard; otherwise a synchronously-throwing loader plus invalidate still lets the stale rejection handle run against newer state.
findings.trigger: A loader that throws synchronously causes the promise returned by startLoad to reject in a later microtask rather than throwing synchronously out of get; combined with no identity check, the later rejection handler mutates `pending` for whatever entry currently occupies the key.
findings.remedy: Keep the async wrapper (it satisfies the sync-throw requirement), and rely on the generation/identity guard so late rejection only affects its own entry.

findings.issue: `once` wrapper is registered as a distinct callback each time, and `remove` (returned by `on` as a filter on the original closure identity) removes the wrapper only if identity matches. Because the wrapper is the pushed entry, `remove()` filters by the wrapper — that part works — but re-entrant emit is not actually protected: the removal closure captured in the wrapper runs `callback(...args)` first, then `remove()`. If `callback` synchronously calls `emit` for the same event, the snapshot taken by that inner emit still contains the wrapper (since `remove()` hasn't run yet) and the once callback fires again, violating 'runs at most once even if it synchronously emits the same event'.
findings.trigger: const e=new Events(); e.once('x',()=>e.emit('x')); e.emit('x'); — the outer emit's snapshot contains the once wrapper, the wrapper invokes the callback, the callback re-emits, the inner emit's snapshot still contains the once wrapper (removal runs only after callback returns), so the once callback executes twice and infinitely recurses.
findings.remedy: Remove the subscription before invoking the callback inside the once wrapper (e.g. call remove() first, then callback(...args)), or track a fired flag so the wrapper is inert on subsequent invocations while still preserving the per-subscription unsubscribe function returned from once.

findings.issue: `once` returns the `remove` from `on`, which is a filter on the wrapper identity. This does satisfy per-subscription unsubscribe for the once case in isolation, but combined with the ordering bug above, 'removing a once subscription before emit prevents it' is only accidentally satisfied: it works because `remove` filters the wrapper, not because once is correctly one-shot. No separate defect independent of the ordering bug, but the correctness of the returned unsubscribe is coupled to the broken wrapper.
findings.trigger: e.once('x', cb); const off = e.once('x', cb); — two wrappers, two subscriptions; off() removes only the second wrapper. This matches the required per-subscription behavior, so no standalone defect; noted for completeness.
findings.remedy: No change needed beyond ensuring the wrapper's self-removal ordering is correct; keep returning the wrapper-scoped remove so per-subscription unsubscribe semantics are preserved.

findings.issue: once listener is not marked as once before invocation; if the callback synchronously emits the same event, the wrapper is still present in the re-entrant emit's snapshot and callback runs again.
findings.trigger: const e=new Events(); e.once('x',()=>e.emit('x')); e.emit('x') invokes callback twice.
findings.remedy: Set a flag / remove the subscription before calling callback inside the once wrapper, so a re-entrant emit from the same start-snapshot cannot match it. E.g. make the wrapper remove itself first (guard against re-removal), then call callback.

findings.issue: on's returned unsubscribe removes all equal callback entries via filter(item => item !== callback), not just the specific subscription. Registering the same callback twice and unsubscribing one leaves the other subscription intact, so this violates the per-subscription unsubscribe requirement.
findings.trigger: const e=new Events(); const cb=()=>{}; const u1=e.on('x',cb); e.on('x',cb); u1(); e.emit('x') — cb still runs, though only one subscription should remain after removing one; here both remain (filter removes neither unique identity, and actually removes none because identity equality matches both instances but filter removes both).
findings.remedy: Track subscriptions as unique objects/ids and remove only the exact subscription returned by that on call.

findings.issue: limit is never validated; non-positive, non-integer, or non-numeric limits are accepted instead of rejecting before any work runs.
findings.trigger: mapLimit(items, 0, work), mapLimit(items, 2.5, work), mapLimit(items, 'x', work), etc.
findings.remedy: At function start, throw/reject if typeof limit !== 'number' or !Number.isInteger(limit) or limit < 1, before invoking work.

findings.issue: work is invoked without the index argument; the request requires each item to be dispatched with its index.
findings.trigger: Any call where work depends on its second argument, e.g. work(item, i).
findings.remedy: Dispatch via .map((item, i) => work(item, i)) over the slice, adjusting the index offset for later batches.

findings.issue: Concurrency is not preserved across batches: each batch is fully awaited before the next starts, and the final partial batch may run with fewer than limit jobs even when more items remain queued.
findings.trigger: items.length not a multiple of limit, or uneven work durations — later jobs wait for the slowest job of the previous batch.
findings.remedy: Implement a worker-pool approach that keeps up to `limit` jobs in flight, launching a new job whenever one settles, until all items are dispatched or an error is observed.

findings.issue: Rejections do not stop launching new work after the first error is observed; every batch continues to be awaited and subsequent batches still launch and run.
findings.trigger: Any work rejection before all batches complete — remaining items keep getting dispatched.
findings.remedy: Track the first observed error, stop scheduling new jobs once set, await settlement of all already-started jobs, then reject with that first error.

findings.issue: Returned Promise may reject with a later error rather than the first observed error, because Promise.all rejects with whichever rejection occurs first within a batch and batching hides earlier errors.
findings.trigger: Multiple rejections across or within batches where the earliest observed error is not the one Promise.all surfaces.
findings.remedy: Capture the first observed rejection explicitly and reject the final promise with that captured error after all in-flight jobs settle.

findings.issue: A synchronous throw inside work propagates directly out of .map before Promise.all is constructed, so the function throws synchronously instead of returning a rejecting Promise, and already-started jobs in that batch may not settle before rejection.
findings.trigger: work called with a function that throws synchronously (e.g. throws immediately for some item).
findings.remedy: Wrap each job invocation in Promise.resolve().then(() => work(item, i)) so sync throws become rejections and are handled uniformly with the first-error tracking.

findings.issue: No validation of `limit`. The spec requires `limit` to be a positive integer and that invalid limits reject before any work runs. The implementation accepts 0, negative, non-integer, NaN, and non-number values without rejecting.
findings.trigger: `mapLimit([1,2,3], 0, work)` — the loop `index < items.length` never advances (index += 0 stays 0), so it returns `[]` after running no work, silently dropping all items instead of rejecting. `mapLimit([1,2], -1, work)` yields a negative step and never terminates (infinite loop / hang). `mapLimit([1,2], 1.5, work)` produces fractional slice indices and non-deterministic chunk sizes. `mapLimit([1,2], 'x', work)` / `NaN` likewise fails the positivity/integer contract.
findings.remedy: At the top of the function, reject invalid limits before doing anything else, e.g. `if (!Number.isInteger(limit) || limit <= 0) throw new RangeError('limit must be a positive integer');`. This also guards against the non-terminating/empty-result cases above since the check runs before the first `Promise.all`.

findings.issue: `work` is invoked as a bare callback, so it receives `(item, arrayIndexWithinChunk, slicedArray)` rather than `(item, index)` as required. Each chunk is a fresh `items.slice(...)`, so the index resets at every batch boundary.
findings.trigger: `mapLimit(['a','b','c'], 2, (item, i) => [item, i])` returns `[['a',0],['b',1],['c',0]]` — the third item receives index 0 instead of the required absolute index 2. Any work function that uses the index for routing, labels, or output positioning gets wrong values.
findings.remedy: Pass the absolute index explicitly: map over chunk positions and call `work(item, index)`, e.g. `items.slice(index, index + limit).map((item, j) => work(item, index + j))`, then `Promise.all` that mapped array.

findings.issue: Failure does not stop launching new work and does not wait for already-started jobs to settle across batches. Batches are strictly sequential and a rejection aborts the loop before later batches, but within the current batch the semantics are only 'whatever Promise.all gives'; there is no first-error capture and no guarantee that all started jobs settle before rejecting.
findings.trigger: If the spec's intended semantics require that once an error is observed no further jobs are launched but in-flight jobs still settle before rejection, this implementation does not implement that contract: it has no error-observation mechanism and relies solely on sequential batching. In addition, because batches are serialized, concurrency never actually reaches `limit` across a batch boundary (a slow item in batch N blocks all of batch N+1), reducing effective concurrency.
findings.remedy: Implement an explicit bounded worker/queue: start up to `limit` jobs, record the first observed error, stop dequeuing on error, `await` all started jobs (`Promise.allSettled`), then reject with the first error. This realizes 'stop launching on observed error', 'all started jobs settle', and true concurrency in one structure.

findings.issue: Batching via `items.slice(...).map(work)` builds intermediate arrays and does not preserve true streaming concurrency; combined with the sequential loop it caps effective parallelism at the batch boundary and duplicates the loop/batch machinery.
findings.trigger: Any workload where item N+1 in the same logical concurrency window is short while a batch item is long: throughput drops versus a maintained worker pool of size `limit`.
findings.remedy: A single bounded-worker loop over a shared index/cursor satisfies concurrency, index passing, error handling, and order in less code than the batch-of-`Promise.all` construction, removing the intermediate slices.

findings.issue: Off-by-one: the loop condition `index <= attempts` with throw at `index === attempts` runs `attempts + 1` operations total, but the contract says `attempts` is the positive integer *total attempt count*. With attempts=3, the function calls operation(0..3), i.e. 4 invocations. The retry/throw boundary also lets index reach `attempts`, so the intended last attempt is never the throw point.
findings.trigger: retry(op, {attempts: 3, signal: ok, sleep}) where op always rejects → op invoked at index 0,1,2,3 (four calls); contract requires three calls and the final error thrown after index 2.
findings.remedy: Iterate over exactly `attempts` attempts, e.g. `for (let index = 0; index < attempts; index += 1)` and throw the final error when `index === attempts - 1`; sleep only between attempts.

findings.issue: Missing validation of `attempts` before doing work. The contract requires validating attempts before any operation/sleep occurs and requires attempts to be a positive integer. The current loop performs operation(0) even for attempts=0, negative, non-integer, or non-number values; with attempts=0 the loop runs once (index 0 <= 0) and never throws based on validation.
findings.trigger: retry(op, {attempts: 0, ...}) executes op(0) instead of rejecting before work; attempts undefined causes `0 <= undefined` to be false and the function silently returns undefined without any operation or clear error.
findings.remedy: At function entry, verify Number.isInteger(attempts) && attempts >= 1 and throw/reject a clear validation error before invoking operation or sleep.

findings.issue: No pre-start cancellation check. The contract requires cancellation before start to reject with signal.reason and prevent further operations. The function immediately invokes operation without inspecting `signal.aborted`, so a signal already aborted before the first call still runs operation(0).
findings.trigger: const ac = new AbortController(); ac.abort(reason); retry(op, {attempts:3, signal: ac.signal, sleep}) → op is invoked despite being cancelled before start.
findings.remedy: Before the loop (and on each iteration before invoking operation), check `signal?.aborted` and reject with signal.reason.

findings.issue: No cancellation handling for sleep rejections or post-resolution cancellation. The contract states a sleep rejection is terminal and must preserve/propagate, and cancellation during sleep or after an operation resolves must reject with signal.reason and prevent further operations. The implementation's `await sleep(10, signal)` is inside the catch block; if sleep rejects, that rejection propagates (good for terminality), but there is no normalization to signal.reason when the rejection is an abort, and there is no explicit guarantee distinguishing cancellation during sleep from an operation error. Also, if operation resolves but the signal was aborted concurrently, the resolved value is returned instead of rejecting with signal.reason.
findings.trigger: Abort during the awaited sleep whose sleep rejects with a non-signal error (or resolves to a DOMException) — the error is not converted to signal.reason as required; or abort races with operation resolution so a resolved operation returns despite post-resolution cancellation.
findings.remedy: Wrap or inspect the sleep rejection: if `signal.aborted`, reject with signal.reason; otherwise propagate the sleep error as terminal. After `await operation`, check `signal?.aborted` and reject with signal.reason before returning.

findings.issue: `signal.reason` is never used anywhere in the implementation. Multiple required behaviors explicitly reject with signal.reason (cancellation before start, during sleep, and after an operation resolves). Their complete absence means the cancellation contract is unimplemented.
findings.trigger: Any abort scenario described in the contract; none produces a rejection with signal.reason.
findings.remedy: Add the signal.aborted checks described above and reject with signal.reason in each case.

findings.issue: No explicit return/throw after the loop. If validation is added or if the loop condition is changed, control can fall through and the function resolves `undefined` instead of rejecting, violating 'the final operation error is preserved' and the retry semantics for canceled/validated paths.
findings.trigger: With attempts undefined the loop body never executes and the function returns undefined rather than throwing the final error or a validation error.
findings.remedy: Ensure every path either returns an operation result, throws the final operation error, or rejects with the validation/cancellation error; add validation to make the fall-through unreachable.

findings.issue: `attempts` is not validated before doing work; invalid values can invoke `operation`, return `undefined`, or run unboundedly.
findings.trigger: `attempts: 0` invokes `operation`; `attempts: -1` returns `undefined`; `attempts: Infinity` loops forever; non-integers alter attempt count.
findings.remedy: At the start of `retry`, reject unless `Number.isInteger(attempts) && attempts > 0`, before any operation or sleep call.

findings.issue: Cancellation before start is ignored; the function does not reject with `signal.reason` and may still call `operation`.
findings.trigger: Call `retry(op, { attempts: 1, signal: alreadyAbortedSignal, sleep })`; `op` is still invoked at index 0.
findings.remedy: After validating `attempts`, check `if (signal?.aborted) throw signal.reason;` before the loop/operation.

findings.issue: Cancellation after an operation resolves is ignored; the function returns the operation result instead of rejecting with `signal.reason`.
findings.trigger: `operation` resolves while `signal.aborted` is true, such as abort occurring during the operation while the operation ignores the signal.
findings.remedy: Store `const result = await operation(index, signal);`, then `if (signal?.aborted) throw signal.reason;`, then `return result;`.

findings.issue: Cancellation during sleep is not enforced by `retry` when the injected `sleep` resolves despite an aborted signal; retry can continue to another operation. Cancellation between a failed operation and sleep is also not checked.
findings.trigger: Signal aborts while `await sleep(10, signal)` is pending and `sleep` resolves, or signal is already aborted after `operation` rejects and before sleep.
findings.remedy: In the catch path, after deciding this is not the final attempt, check `if (signal?.aborted) throw signal.reason;` before and after `await sleep(10, signal)`; sleep rejections already propagate as terminal.

findings.issue: Duplicate target names are not rejected before any store call; applyBatch proceeds to snapshot and writes.
findings.trigger: applyBatch(store, [{name:'a',value:'1'},{name:'a',value:'2'}])
findings.remedy: Before calling snapshot, build a Set of change.name; if size !== changes.length, throw (reject) immediately with a duplicate-name error.

findings.issue: On write failure, only names already successfully written are restored; the failed target and not-yet-written targets are never restored, so a write that mutated then threw leaves that target mutated.
findings.trigger: store.write mutates name 'b' then throws; 'b' is not in written and is never rolled back.
findings.remedy: Rollback all snapshot entries (in reverse snapshot/before order), attempting restoration for every target including the failed one and unvisited ones.

findings.issue: Rollback restores in reverse order of successfully written names instead of reverse order over all original targets, so failed/not-yet-written targets are omitted and ordering is wrong.
findings.trigger: changes = [a,b,c]; write of b mutates then throws; expected restoration c,b,a but only a is restored.
findings.remedy: Iterate the pre-capture snapshot array in reverse (for (let i = before.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)) and restore each entry.

findings.issue: If a rollback write/remove throws, applyBatch stops rollback and rethrows, violating required continued restoration and AggregateError semantics.
findings.trigger: store.write during rollback of one target throws; remaining targets are not attempted and no AggregateError is produced.
findings.remedy: Collect errors: push original write error, then attempt every restoration in reverse order, pushing each rollback error in observation order; if any rollback error occurred, throw new AggregateError(errors, message), else rethrow the original error.

findings.issue: Snapshot failures are not isolated from writes as an explicit no-write guarantee; wrapping snapshot in the same try that performs writes risks partial writes if snapshot logic were interleaved.
findings.trigger: If snapshot ever performs side effects or is moved inside the write loop, a snapshot failure could coexist with writes.
findings.remedy: Keep snapshot fully outside the try that performs writes; call snapshot before the try/catch so a snapshot rejection propagates before any store.write/remove is invoked.

findings.issue: Missing validation that changes is an array / that each change has name and value; interface contract expects strings.
findings.trigger: applyBatch(store, null) or change without value throws a TypeError inside map rather than a deliberate rejection.
findings.remedy: Validate input shape before snapshot, or document/accept that TypeError is the rejection for malformed changes.

findings.issue: Partial-failure rollback only restores targets that were successfully written (`written`), not ALL targets, and never restores the failed or not-yet-written targets. Request requires restoring ALL targets to their original value or absence in reverse order, including the failed and not-yet-written target.
findings.trigger: A write mutates the store and then throws (e.g. store.write appears in `written` only after it returns, so a throwing write is never pushed). Example: changes = [{name:'a',value:'1'},{name:'b',value:'2'},{name:'c',value:'3'}]; store.write('b','2') mutates 'b' then throws. `written` = ['a']; rollback only restores 'a'. 'b' is left mutated, 'c' untouched (correct for c) but 'b' remains dirty. Additionally a target with name 'c' that was never attempted is not restored even if a later write had mutated it.
findings.remedy: Snapshot all targets first (already done via `before`), then on failure iterate over ALL snapshot entries in reverse order, invoking the restore (write original value if it existed, else remove) for every target regardless of whether its write was recorded. Wrap each restoration so a rollback failure is captured rather than aborting the loop.

findings.issue: Rollback failures abort the loop and the original error, so remaining restorations are skipped and the required AggregateError is never produced. Request: if rollback also fails, keep trying remaining restorations and reject an AggregateError whose errors start with the original write error followed by rollback errors in observation order.
findings.trigger: Any store.write/remove during rollback throws. The `for` loop's `await store.write(...)` rejection propagates immediately (the original error is discarded) and subsequent targets are not restored.
findings.remedy: Collect errors into an array seeded with the original error, push each rollback error in order while continuing the loop, and after the loop throw new AggregateError(errors, ...). If no rollback errors occurred, rethrow the original error object unchanged.

findings.issue: Snapshot failure handling: the requirement says snapshot failures perform no writes. In the current implementation `snapshot` is awaited before the try block, so a snapshot rejection propagates without writes. This behavior is correct, but it is not guarded — if the code is later refactored to move snapshot inside the try, the catch would incorrectly attempt rollback.
findings.trigger: Only a latent/regression risk; current code passes. No concrete failing input today.
findings.remedy: Keep `snapshot` outside the try/catch (or document the invariant) so snapshot errors bypass any rollback path.

findings.issue: Duplicate target names are not rejected before any store call. Request: duplicate target names are invalid and must reject before any store call.
findings.trigger: changes = [{name:'a',value:'1'},{name:'a',value:'2'}]; current code calls snapshot (store.has/read) and then store.write twice on 'a' before any duplicate check.
findings.remedy: Validate uniqueness of `changes.map(c=>c.name)` before invoking snapshot, and reject (e.g. TypeError/Error) without touching the store.

findings.issue: Snapshot uses `has` then `read`; if `has` returns true but `read` returns undefined/absent (or `has`/`read` are inconsistent), the snapshot records `value: undefined` with `exists: true`, and rollback would later `write(name, undefined)`, violating the 'all values are strings' invariant and possibly corrupting the target.
findings.trigger: A store implementation where `has` returns true yet `read` yields undefined (race or inconsistent adapter). Then `item.exists` is true and `store.write(name, undefined)` is called during rollback.
findings.remedy: Either treat `read` result as the source of truth (exists = value !== undefined) or explicitly guard/validate that an existing target's value is a string before rollback writes.

findings.issue: `before.find(...)` inside the rollback loop is O(n) per target and relies on name identity rather than positional correspondence; with the required full-set reverse iteration this becomes unnecessary indirection.
findings.trigger: Large batches produce quadratic lookup cost; also obscures the requirement that restoration order is reverse snapshot order over ALL targets.
findings.remedy: Iterate `before` directly with an index/reverse copy (e.g. `for (let i = before.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { const item = before[i]; ... }`) so each target is restored exactly once in reverse order without lookups.

findings.issue: The function does not preserve unrelated top-level properties correctly and violates several stated requirements: it hardcodes a default theme when none should be invented, drops other display fields, mutates semantics of version handling, fails to reject unknown/missing versions, and does not deep-clone schema 2 inputs or legacy settings.
findings.trigger: Calling `migrate(settings)` on a schema 1 object: (a) if `display` has fields like `{contrast: 'high'}`, they are replaced by only `{theme: ...}`; (b) if no top-level `theme` exists, it invents `theme: "dark"` instead of leaving display without a theme; (c) if top-level `theme` is an empty string `""`, `||` falls through to `"dark"` instead of preserving the legacy empty string; (d) any `version` value is overwritten to 2 rather than rejecting unknown versions; (e) no check rejects missing `version`; (f) schema 2 inputs are not cloned and nested `display` (and any nested objects in settings) are effectively replaced for top-level shallow copy while other nested object values are shared by reference.
findings.remedy: Implement a version-checking migration: require `settings.version` to be exactly 1 or 2 and return an error/rejection for other cases; for version 2, return a deep clone (e.g. structured clone) with no other change; for version 1, shallow/deep-clone preserving all top-level keys and all `display` fields, then set `display.theme` from the legacy `theme` only when the legacy property exists (using `hasOwnProperty`, preserving empty string); delete the top-level `theme` key after migration; set `version: 2`; do not introduce a default theme when none exists.

findings.issue: The implementation ignores settings.version and never rejects missing or unknown versions.
findings.trigger: migrate({}) or migrate({version:3}) returns a schema-2-like object instead of rejecting.
findings.remedy: Validate that settings.version is exactly 1 or 2; throw for missing or any other version before transformation.

findings.issue: Schema 2 input is not returned as an independent deep clone unchanged; it is always rewritten and nested objects are not cloned.
findings.trigger: migrate({version:2, display:{theme:'light', scale:2}, plugin:{a:1}}) changes/replaces display and result.plugin shares the input plugin object.
findings.remedy: Add a version === 2 branch that returns structuredClone(settings) or an equivalent independent deep clone without modification.

findings.issue: Existing display fields are discarded because display is replaced with only a theme property.
findings.trigger: migrate({version:1, display:{theme:'old', other:1}, theme:'new'}) loses display.other.
findings.remedy: Clone settings.display when present, then set or omit theme on that clone instead of replacing the whole display object.

findings.issue: The legacy theme expression uses ||, so an empty string legacy theme is treated as absent.
findings.trigger: migrate({version:1, theme:''}) yields display.theme 'dark' instead of preserving ''.
findings.remedy: Check own-property presence with Object.hasOwn(settings, 'theme') or hasOwnProperty.call(settings, 'theme'), and assign the value even when it is an empty string.

findings.issue: A default dark theme is invented when no legacy top-level theme exists.
findings.trigger: migrate({version:1, display:{other:1}}) returns display.theme 'dark'.
findings.remedy: Only add display.theme if the own top-level theme property exists; otherwise preserve the display object without inventing a theme.

findings.issue: The top-level theme property is not removed from the migrated schema 1 result, so it is copied rather than moved.
findings.trigger: migrate({version:1, theme:'light'}) returns both top-level theme and display.theme.
findings.remedy: Destructure or otherwise exclude the own top-level theme when building the migrated schema 1 result, without mutating the input.

findings.issue: Nested objects are shared with the result because the implementation only shallow-spreads preserved properties.
findings.trigger: const input={version:1, plugin:{a:1}}; const result=migrate(input); result.plugin.a=2 also changes input.plugin.a.
findings.remedy: Deep clone preserved values into the result, e.g. structuredClone, so no nested object reference is shared with any input.

findings.issue: Arrays are handled by the object branch, so arrays and objects are not distinguishable in the canonical string.
findings.trigger: canonicalKey([1,2]) === canonicalKey({'0':1,'1':2}) gives '0:1,1:2'; canonicalKey([]) === canonicalKey({}) gives ''.
findings.remedy: Branch on Array.isArray(value) and encode arrays with a distinct array delimiter/prefix, e.g. '[' + value.map(canonicalKey).join(',') + ']', while objects use a distinct object encoding.

findings.issue: Primitive values are serialized via String(value), losing the required distinctions between strings, numbers, booleans, and null.
findings.trigger: canonicalKey('1') === canonicalKey(1) === '1'; canonicalKey('null') === canonicalKey(null) === 'null'; canonicalKey('true') === canonicalKey(true) === 'true'.
findings.remedy: Tag primitives by type, e.g. return 's:' + JSON.stringify(value) for strings, 'n:' + String(value) for numbers, 'b:' + String(value) for booleans, and 'z' for null.

findings.issue: Object key/value boundaries are ambiguous because keys and values are concatenated without escaping or length-delimiting.
findings.trigger: canonicalKey({'a:b':'c'}) === canonicalKey({'a':'b:c'}) === 'a:b:c'; separators inside strings/keys can similarly collide.
findings.remedy: Use an unambiguous entry encoding, e.g. length-prefix the key and canonical value (or JSON.stringify the key and length-delimit the value) before joining entries.

findings.issue: canonicalKey collapses distinct types and values into identical strings, violating the requirement to preserve distinctions between strings/numbers/booleans/null and between arrays/objects. Arrays are treated as objects (typeof [] === "object"), so [1,2] and {"0":1,"1":2} both canonicalize to "0:1,1:2". Scalars lose their type: true, "true", and the string literal produce "true"; 1 and "1" both produce "1"; null and "null" both produce "null".
findings.trigger: canonicalKey([1,2]) === canonicalKey({"0":1,"1":2}) returns true. canonicalKey(true) === canonicalKey("true") returns true. canonicalKey(null) === canonicalKey("null") returns true. canonicalKey(1) === canonicalKey("1") returns true.
findings.remedy: Branch on array vs plain object explicitly (Array.isArray) and prefix or wrap values with type tags (e.g. "s:", "n:", "b:", "null:", "a[...]", "o{...}") so type and container identity are encoded before joining.

findings.issue: Array order is joined with the same separator used for object entries and without an array delimiter, so array order only distinguishes sequences whose element strings differ. More fundamentally, the object entry encoding key + ":" + value allows key/value boundaries to be forged by keys or values containing ":" and ",". A key like "a:1,b" with value 2 can produce the same string as separate entries.
findings.trigger: canonicalKey({"a": "b", "a:b": "c"}) and crafted keys/values containing ',' and ':' yield identical canonical strings because the raw key and value strings are concatenated without length-prefixing or escaping.
findings.remedy: Use an unambiguous encoding: length-prefix keys and values, or escape reserved separators (backslash/quote), and emit explicit array brackets and object braces plus type tags so no concatenation of raw strings can collide.

findings.issue: Object entries are joined with ',' and keys with ':' without escaping, and arrays also join with ',' without a distinguishing prefix, so a nested empty object/array or order-sensitive structure is not faithfully represented. An empty array [] and empty object {} both return "" (empty string), and an empty string value also returns "".
findings.trigger: canonicalKey([]) === canonicalKey({}) === canonicalKey("") === "" returns true.
findings.remedy: Encode containers with explicit delimiters/tags (e.g. "[]" for empty array, "{}" for empty object) and type-tag scalars so empty containers and empty strings remain distinct.

findings.issue: Accessing value[key] via bracket notation is safe for __proto__ as an own data key, but the code does not restrict traversal to own enumerable data properties in a robust way for inherited/prototype concerns; more directly, the implementation relies on Object.keys which is correct for own enumerable string keys, so the stated __proto__ requirement is largely satisfied. However, the sort is over raw key strings, and the canonical form is ambiguous as above, so deterministic ordering is only partially met.
findings.trigger: canonicalKey(Object.assign(Object.create(null), {"__proto__": 1})) and similar rely on own-key behavior; Object.keys does include an own "__proto__" data key, so ordering is deterministic, but ambiguity from finding 1/2 still applies.
findings.remedy: Keep Object.keys for own keys, but fix the encoding ambiguity (findings 1-3) so the sort actually yields a unique canonical form.

findings.issue: Empty pages with a non-null nextCursor are treated as terminal: `cursor = page.items.length ? page.nextCursor : null;` stops the loop whenever a page has zero items, even though the request explicitly says empty pages can carry a next cursor and must continue.
findings.trigger: fetchPage(null) returns {items: [], nextCursor: "c1"}; the loop sets cursor=null and returns an empty array without ever fetching "c1".
findings.remedy: Set the cursor from the page unconditionally (`cursor = page.nextCursor;`) and let the `while (cursor !== null)` condition be the sole stop rule.

findings.issue: No detection of a repeated non-null next cursor. The loop will re-issue fetches for a cursor that was already used, looping indefinitely on a cyclic provider instead of rejecting before the duplicate fetch.
findings.trigger: fetchPage returns nextCursor "a" on one page and nextCursor "a" again on the following page; collect calls fetchPage("a") repeatedly and never terminates.
findings.remedy: Track seen cursors (e.g. a Set containing null plus each issued cursor) and reject/throw before calling fetchPage with a cursor already fetched.

findings.issue: `items.push(...page.items)` uses spread, which is subject to the argument-length limit and will throw a RangeError for very large pages; it also relies on the source arrays, though it does not mutate them.
findings.trigger: A page with a very large `items` array (order tens to hundreds of thousands) passed to push via spread exceeds the engine's max-args limit.
findings.remedy: Accumulate with a plain loop or `items = items.concat(page.items)` (or push per element) to avoid the spread arity limit.

findings.issue: mergeItems builds a Map keyed by id and keeps the last occurrence, so it does not implement 'highest revision wins' and does not retain first-occurrence order after a later duplicate with a newer revision.
findings.trigger: items = [{id:"x",revision:1,value:"old"},{id:"x",revision:2,value:"new"}] -> Map keeps the revision-2 entry; but items = [{id:"x",revision:2},{id:"x",revision:1}] -> Map overwrites with revision 1, yielding the lower revision, and a duplicate that appears later also shifts ordering relative to pure first occurrence.
findings.remedy: Iterate in order, keep a Map from id to the current best entry, and replace only when the incoming revision is strictly greater than the stored revision (and keep the first value on equal revisions).

findings.issue: Equal-revision tie handling is unspecified by the implementation and contradicts 'retain the first value': a Map overwrite on equal revision would keep the later value.
findings.trigger: items = [{id:"x",revision:5,value:"first"},{id:"x",revision:5,value:"second"}] -> Map stores "second".
findings.remedy: On equal revision, retain the existing entry (do not overwrite), preserving first occurrence and first value.
